We have explored this method in detail, specifically in relation to speech recognition systems that operate outside of the trained language. In our experiments, we established a dataset called Bilingual Corpus Finest Split, which enables the evaluation of speech recognition transfer learning between multiple languages. Our results indicated that speech recognition transfer learning is feasible with reduced data, particularly when using a pre-trained model. We also discovered that systems trained on finer-grained data layers achieve higher accuracy. In the case of languages where only little information is available, starting with coarse-grained data layers yields better results. Our findings demonstrate that speech recognition transfer learning between languages can be very effective, especially in scenarios with limited data.

Twitch live streams represent a complex social network where users can share their thoughts and engage with each other. Evaluating the effectiveness of node embedding methods is crucial to identify meaningful patterns within this social graph. Existing evaluation metrics for node embedding methods are typically applied to classification and link prediction tasks. We propose a novel evaluation framework that assesses the structural role-based node embedding methods for social network analysis. Our framework utilizes a dataset we've created, which includes proximity information between users and is specifically designed to test the accuracy of these methods. We've tested our evaluation framework on a dataset we've named "Twitch Players" and obtained results that indicate a method's performance on the evaluation framework doesn't always align with its performance on classification and link prediction tasks.

Our study proposes that a complex, recently reported resonance at $1500$, which is likely composed of multiple components and is linked to various $B$-decays, such as $B\to \pi K K$ and $B\to K K \bar{K}$, might instead be a manifestation of the $\rho^0(1450)$ pole that is present in the $B\to \pi \rho$ decay chain. We based our analysis on a comprehensive examination of $B\to \pi K K$ and $B\to K K \bar{K}$ decay data from BaBar and Belle, as well as direct $B\to \pi \rho$ decay data from BaBar and Belle, and LHCb. By employing an advanced fitting approach that accounts for multiple fit parameters, we observed that the presence of the $\rho^0(1450)$ pole fits the data exceptionally well for all relevant decay channels. We estimated the mass and width of the $\rho^0(1450)$ to be $1451.8 \pm 4.3$ MeV and $106.1 \pm 9.8$ MeV, respectively. Notably, we found that the branching fractions for $B\to \pi K^+ K^-$ and $B\to K^+ K^- K^-$ to the $\rho^0(1450)$ final state are $1.106 \pm 0

Recent cosmological measurements suggest the presence of a missing mass component in the universe, which could be explained by Dark Energy or an alternate solution. In this study, we propose an alternative explanation, suggesting that Dark Matter is composed of Primordial Black Holes formed during the early universe's inflationary period. To support this theory, we base our model on an eternally existing universe with an ever-expanding cosmos. We demonstrate that in this model, an instability in the early universe leads to the creation of small Black Holes during the symmetry-breaking period, which then make up the universe's Dark Matter. Our calculation shows that if the universe's scalar curvature is highly negative, these Primordial Black Holes can constitute the required 31% Dark Matter fraction needed to stabilize the universe's motion. Additionally, we examine the Swampland program's constraints on our theory and find that our model satisfies the "gravitational wave prediction" constraint but falls short of meeting the "degenerate multiple inflationary eternally existing universes" constraint when considering the effects of gravitational waves on gravitational wave spectra. Our model also complies with the "primordial black hole resonant generation" constraint, meeting the necessary conditions set by the standard model of cosmology, and exhibiting resonant generation features that could be verified through gravitational wave spectra in the future. Our hypothesis is thus compatible with the Swampland program except for one constraint.

A key issue in Series Elastic Actuators (SEAs) is the accurate estimation of the transmission force, which is crucial for developing reliable force-controlled robotic systems. This study presents a novel, robust force estimation approach for SEAs, utilizing a transmission force observer based on the continuous extended Kalman filter, which can effectively handle both external disturbances and SEA nonlinear characteristics. However, this approach has a significant drawback: it requires the knowledge of the stochastic characteristics of the measurement and process noises, which is often impossible to obtain in practice. To address this challenge, this study develops a discrete time variant of the extended Kalman filter force observer, which can provide an accurate estimation of the transmission force without relying on prior knowledge of the noise characteristics. Although this approach initially seems computationally efficient, it actually has a significant drawback: it may lead to divergence. To mitigate this issue, this study proposes a practical approach involving the addition of a damping term to the SEA's mechanical equation, which facilitates stable force regulation using the discrete time variant of the extended Kalman filter force observer. This approach is experimentally validated using a robotic arm featuring an SEA-based end effector, which demonstrates the efficacy of the proposed discrete time variant of the extended Kalman filter force observer for transmission force estimation in SEA systems.

A distinct feature of living matter is exhibited by cell membranes that are characterized as dynamic rafts, capable of adapting to various situations through their rapid movement. In an effort to understand the structure of these rafts, we use a mathematical model that combines flory-like theory with a specific approach to examine their thermal properties. In a recent paper, it was shown that this model leads to a comprehensive understanding of how the size of raft clusters is distributed. Building on this previous work, we have obtained new insights into the model's parameters required for raft structures that are isolated from one another. In addition, we have derived an accurate method for calculating the average distance between these isolated raft structures.

We've analyzed a range of SU(Nc) gauge theories in 3D lattices that incorporate scalar fields with the capacity for multiparameter interactions. These multiparameter interactions can be broadly categorized into two types: those that mix up to Ns Nc fundamental representations of the gauge group and those that are only accessible in systems with a higher number of flavors. Through both lattice Monte Carlo simulations and exact special cases using lattice Hamiltonian formulation, we've studied the phase diagrams of these models, focusing particularly on their Higgs phases. When the scalar fields have negative mass terms that aren't too large, these models often exhibit Higgs phase transitions. However, when these mass terms become sufficiently positive, these models generally transition into charge density wave phases. Additionally, in models with a higher number of flavors, gauge group symmetries can be reduced even when there are large differences between the mass parameters of the various fundamental representations, leading to phase transitions into Higgs phases. For instance, in SU(Nc) gauge theories with Nf flavors of massless scalar fields, we've found evidence of (Nf/Nc)-folded charge density wave phases, where symmetries are reduced by a factor of Nf/Nc in the representation group.

Our novel TD learning approach is designed to minimize the time spent by a marine robot to reach its target, with the caveat that it must follow a predetermined coastline path. This problem is particularly challenging due to the robot's limited range of motion and the complexity of modeling their environment through a stochastic process that captures the dynamics of the ocean's tides. To overcome these obstacles, we modeled the system as a Gaussian process and developed a range-sensitivity TD algorithm to optimize the robot's performance within the confines of its movement capabilities. Interestingly, we discovered that the optimal policy can be achieved through a sparse representation, allowing us to implement the algorithm on a real-time system. Notably, our method excels in comparison to state-of-the-art TD algorithms, yielding a significant improvement in the robot's efficiency according to our experimental results.

This paper explores the concept of arranging networks with limited depth, building upon a previously established framework by Lin and Winograd. We develop two novel circuit configurations that facilitate linear transformations in O(n) time, within three layers. These circuits leverage n processors and have an overall size of n. We demonstrate the efficacy of these arrangements in solving linear systems with multiple right-hand sides and matrix multiplication problems. Notably, our models outperform the previously known deep arrangements by Barash and Galil, specifically for systems with multiple right-hand sides and matrix multiplication problems.

We develop a theoretical framework for a static and spherically symmetric relativistic star consisting of a dual-fluid composite, made up of an anisotropic fluid component and a radiation fluid. By formulating the stress-energy momentum tensor as a linear combination of the stress-energy momentum tensors of the respective fluids, we establish the conditions under which this dual-fluid configuration can be represented as a perfect fluid with a specific energy density and pressure. Furthermore, we derive anisotropic energy density expressions for the anisotropic fluid and relativistic stars, respectively. Additionally, we investigate the impact of radial and tangential pressure gradients on the anisotropic energy density of the anisotropic fluid and relativistic stars.

The observed spiral structure in a galaxy resembles a grand design spiral, consisting of multiple spiral arms. However, determining the number of spiral arms in the Milky Way remains a topic of debate. Recent studies suggest that a multi-component galaxy, similar to the Milky Way, has spiral arms formed by fast-moving star populations and a majority of its stars. Utilizing the Besan\char43{}on et al. (2003) modeling of the Milky Way, we simulate a galaxy with a similar mass and composition to investigate the structure of its spiral arms. Leveraging the GALAXY\char43{}VIEW software, we create a spiral arm model that undergoes dynamic evolution, inspired by the pattern speed and arm pitch angle of the Milky Way. Results from our simulations reveal that a multi-component Milky~Way-like galaxy features two distinct spiral arms formed by its star populations.

Strong magnetic fields can significantly impact galaxy mergers by affecting how gas and stars are rearranged during the merger. This study uses high-resolution simulations to analyze the effect of magnetic fields on major galaxy mergers, considering two possible scenarios where the strength of the magnetic field varies - either it is strong in the galaxies but weak in the surrounding intergalactic medium, or it is strong in both. In the first scenario, the strong magnetic field in the galaxies causes their gas and stellar discs to become more irregularly shaped, affecting the ultraviolet light emitted by oxygen and other elements. However, the distinctive spectral lines from these elements remain largely the same. In the second scenario, the strong magnetic field in the galaxies has a similar impact, but it also affects the surrounding intergalactic medium, causing the galaxies to sink further into their halos due to their increased resistance to motion. As a result, the galaxies experience a more significant interaction, leading to even more irregularly shaped gas and stellar discs. Ultimately, the magnetic fields play a key role in determining the final shape of the merger and the characteristics of any resulting stellar formation.

Our solution to the intense issue of predicting coronavirus severity level from radiography images is presented in this research paper.  We take a data-driven approach and address several challenges inherent in machine learning technology.  To provide a high-performing model, we propose an infection-aware 3D classification framework based on contrastive mixup classification.  By conducting extensive experiments on a large dataset of coronavirus severity levels, our classification framework is consistently shown to achieve superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques.

Leveraging neural machine translation to correct grammatical errors across various languages has been a focus for research on translation-based grammatical error correction (GEC). Since each language has its own distinct characteristics, zero-shot and few-shot domain transfer in GEC is particularly challenging. To achieve this, we introduce a novel, multi-domain approach to GEC, based on models that learn from meta-learning. By applying a controller module that selects language-specific parameters for a neural machine translation model, our approach enables near-zero-shot GEC in new languages. To further improve performance, we implemented a method for transferring knowledge in few-shot scenarios. In experiments, our results showed that our proposed approach achieves highly accurate outcomes compared to current state-of-the-art methods on the NUS GEC Evaluation data sets for Chinese, English and six other languages.

Rounding is an established technique used to handle sensitive data, particularly when counting the number of times people have experienced a certain event. Researchers typically estimate unknown counts based on rounded averages from a random sample of those events. The standard method used to estimate these counts is the rounded average method. However, we show that this approach has a bias that is significant enough to impact policy decisions, especially in cases where the rounded values are far from the actual counts. We demonstrate an alternative method, the rounded mass method, which takes into account the ambiguity of rounded data and provides more accurate estimates of these counts. The new method involves using the rounded averages as probabilities and estimating the counts through direct calculation, which is feasible with common statistical software. We show through simulations that the bias in the standard method increases as the number of possible values in each category (ambiguity) increases and that the new method performs better in terms of precision. The study also finds that the standard method tends to underestimate large counts and overestimate small counts, resulting in a bias that is not always consistent with what would be expected (as predicted by the fuzzy regression approach). The article concludes by highlighting the practical applications of the new method, which is less expensive to implement than the standard method, especially in cases with high ambiguity.

Researchers investigated the crystallography and magnetic character of the honeycomb compound GdInO3, which they synthesized using a high-temperature solid-state method. By analyzing its structural and magnetic properties, they discovered that GdInO3 has a lattice structure composed of two-dimensional honeycomb cells, located between two-dimensional and three-dimensional parity boundaries. In this study, they examined the magnetic properties of this compound through both direct and indirect mean-field theoretical models, and found that a specific average-field approach more accurately represents its properties. Additionally, they discovered that both the indirect approach and the specific average-field approach fail to explain the observed shift in magnetic transition temperature, and that both models require adjustments to capture this phenomenon.

The classic problem of allocating divisible goods among a group of selfless agents has been extensively studied in various fields, including economics, mathematics, and computer science, with multiple approaches to find efficient and fair solutions on the Vickrey-Christoffel matrix. However, real-world scenarios often involve indivisible goods with strategic behavior from agents, making the allocation process more complex and multifaceted. This paper focuses on finding exact and approximate algorithms to resolve this challenge, particularly in environments where agents act rationally and independently, with an interest in rationally finding equilibriums that satisfy fairness criteria such as envy-free and fair mobility. This study presents the first fully accurate algorithm for allocating one good to two agents, as well as the first fair algorithm for allocating one good to three agents, and shows that envy-free algorithms are possible for up to five agents, though an envy-free algorithm was previously known for this number of agents.

In our research, we diverge from the standard practice in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) of employing a direct, one-to-one mapping between source and target domains. Instead, we utilize stochastic transformations to account for the variations within each domain. This approach allows us to achieve better results by utilizing labeled source data and unlabeled target data to produce multiple discrete representations of each domain. We can then conduct a thorough comparison of these representations to devise more accurate and diverse transformation methods. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method by developing a prominent model that successfully adapts domains without assuming a direct correlation between the source and target domains. We conduct multiple experiments to validate our approach, showing significant improvements over the current state-of-the-art methods in domain adaptation across multiple domains and domains with significant disparities.

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. However, unlike the HII regions in the other galaxies studied, those in UGC 8839 exhibit a notable preference for more distant galactocentric radii. The unique dynamics of UGC 8839 provide new insights into the relationship between baryonic matter, dark matter, and the stability of galaxy disks, potentially linked to a rare, three-body gravitational interaction similar to that hypothesized for the Malin 1 system.

Researchers propose using paleo-detectors, an experimental technique, to detect dark matter. Unlike conventional detectors, which require massive and expensive set-ups, paleo-detectors utilize naturally occurring rocks with deep geological history that contain tiny damage tracks from dark matter interactions. Thanks to advancements in microscopy and the ability to study samples over billions of years, paleo-detectors can potentially offer more sensitive detection at significantly lower costs. This could significantly expand the range of sensitivity in dark matter research. Using updated analytical methods, scientists have simulated the capabilities of paleo-detectors under various conditions and found them robust against inaccuracies in age measurements and the composition of samples. Even with relatively high concentrations of radioactive contaminants, the sensitivity of paleo-detectors can surpass current limits, offering the possibility to detect dark matter interactions below existing detection thresholds, even when masses are less than ten GeV.

This paper introduces a novel form of attack in remote database management, which takes advantage of a common pattern to synchronize updates. Specifically, an adversary can determine updates made by a user by analyzing the changes made to a record that contains both the user's information and update history. To address this threat, DP-Sync is a new differential privacy framework for safeguarding update histories against malicious query patterns. This framework incorporates a unique new mechanism called Clustering Noise, which enables achieving the optimal privacy goal set by the LPB bound for a specific case of synchronizing updates. To verify the effectiveness of DP-Sync, the paper includes results from several practical experiments and a performance analysis of its components.

The extensive use of Machine Learning (ML) in high-security sectors necessitates a thorough understanding of its capabilities and limitations. Recently, research into ML model robustness has revealed the vulnerability of models like Random Forest to crafted attacks. Although various adversarial analysis methods have been proposed, there is a noticeable lack of understanding regarding why certain features are susceptible to manipulation. To address this knowledge gap, we propose a distinctive approach for evaluating feature significance in Random Forest. By utilizing the proposed approach in conjunction with MUC values, we are able to identify the most risk-prone features across different datasets, providing valuable insights that can be utilized to enhance the forest's resilience and counter adverse effects. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates the efficacy of this approach in providing actionable suggestions for optimizing model performance in the presence of adversarial attacks.

Minimally invasive surgery has emerged as a highly effective treatment, allowing for accurate targeting and real-time visual feedback during operations. However, the limited field-of-view and difficulty in detecting moving instruments pose significant challenges for medical professionals. In this paper, we focus on the task of automatically identifying surgical instruments from video feedback in real-time. To achieve this, we employ a novel approach that leverages deep learning, specifically a multi-task convolutional neural network, to directly detect instruments from video frames. Our experiments, involving the training and testing of 6000 frames on the laparoscopic instrument dataset, reveal our method's superiority over alternative techniques and demonstrated real-time performance with only 20ms latency.

Current re-identification methods rely heavily on labeled data, which can be difficult to obtain in large quantities. Unlike identification, re-identification involves ranking a set of potential identities by confidence. A new large-scale unsupervised individual re-identification approach has been developed, utilizing contrastive loss functions to learn identity-specific information from unlabeled groups. Essentially, this technique treats two random individuals as opposites, learning to identify similarities within groups and differentiate between groups. Moreover, it incorporates a probe network to detect identity by comparing pairs of people, either within a group or across multiple groups, ultimately producing a metric that ranks identities accurately.

This research introduces an innovative threshold assessment GARCH model that uses realized volatility to forecast tail risks. The new model's parameters, including those for the GARCH and Extreme Value Theory components, are estimated using a range of methods within a Bayesian framework. Specifically, an approach was developed to estimate parameters by drawing random samples from their underlying distribution. The study demonstrated that the proposed model outperforms existing alternatives in forecasting tail risks and related risk measures. The findings are verified using multiple datasets and stress testing was conducted on the model's ability to predict tail risks. The study's results indicate that the proposed model yields more accurate predictions and can be applied to guide strategic decisions in practice.

Recent findings from global pulsar timing arrays suggest a nano-Hertz gravitational wave background signal remains elusive in current data. Nevertheless, enhanced datasets are expected to yield statistically significant evidence in the future. This study endeavors to eliminate the limitation of expensive maximum likelihood calculations in the context of gravitational wave data analysis. By "sturdy" in this context, we refer to models with a gravitational wave spectrum that exhibits a clear feature, such as a pulsar pair's unique signal resonance. A new statistical approach is developed to estimate the parameters of these models efficiently. To test its effectiveness, the estimation method was applied to two simulated data sets, and the results revealed that even with relatively small datasets, precision comparable to maximum likelihood was achievable. Furthermore, this study demonstrates that applying this technique to the current data set PULSARALaCarte dataset yields an estimation for the gravitational wave spectral density around 2.6 ten to the power of negative 10, unlike the maximum likelihood calculation's ability to match the actual parameters.

Using lattice QCD, a method to connect quark and hadron currents through correlation functions is demonstrated. With this approach, the complete set of two-quark correlations, representing all possible combinations of quark and antiquark polarizations, is shown to be sufficient to derive the isospin-symmetric mass of the pion. Although this mass can also be determined through a simpler average of the pion's momentum-dependent masses, our approach offers a more versatile framework for investigating hadron properties, capable of handling more complex phenomena such as spin polarization or form factors, across a broad range of momentum scales.

Evaluating protoplanetary disk evolution is closely tied to understanding how
mass accretion rates are influenced by a star and its disk properties.
However, accurately using observed mass accretion rates in this context
requires a deep understanding of how these rates are affected by other factors,
especially in conjunction with spectroscopic stellar properties.
Such considerations are especially crucial when analyzing the outcomes of
complex physical processes affecting disk development, such as the transition
from turbulent to laminar disk flow.
Our previous research revealed that stars with the lowest mass accretion rates
in the PENELLOPE survey were more massive than expected, given their luminosity,
suggesting that certain variables could distort the relationship between mass
accretion and stellar properties.
To further investigate these variables, we examined the variability of XX Cha,
a star exhibiting unusually high globular photospheric features and an abnormal
accretion pattern.
Our analysis showed that XX Cha's observed mass accretion is overestimated by at
least 5 times due to its unusual variability, impacting the interpretation of
its place within the broader T Tauri population.
As a result, XX Cha no longer stands out as an exception in the mass accretion
rate distribution when its variability is considered.
This discovery has implications for using survey data to understand variability
behaviour in T Tauri stars and the potential for bias in analysis focused on
average values, such as the distribution of mass accretion rates.

The concept of opportunity inequality can be viewed through the lens of chance inequality, which is influenced by both natural opportunities and artificial structures. The interplay between these factors and their impact on individual chances of success are complex, especially when considering the role of luck. The opportunity inequality framework, however, helps to break down the chances of success into their component probabilities, thus providing a more nuanced understanding. The interplay between these probabilities, however, introduces a cyclical dynamic, where the redistribution of income can, in turn, affect the probability of success, ultimately influencing the chances of survival. The resulting steady-state equilibrium, where survival probabilities are equal, hides the inequality present in these chances, as it does not account for opportunities beyond mere survival. The opportunity inequality framework also reveals the limitations of policies aimed at reducing income inequality, as these policies may have little impact on actual chances of success. The chance inequality framework, on the other hand, does consider these opportunities and highlights how chance affects the chances of success, creating a dynamic where survival is assured but greater chances may be unattainable. The combination of these perspectives provides a more comprehensive understanding of opportunity inequality, incorporating both structural and probabilistic elements.

Removing central subvarieties from a partial flag variety Flu+, we obtain a 'banner variety'. Quantum K-theory studies the ring generated by Schubert classes in K-theory of these spaces, with relations derived from stable point currents and mixed Hodge equations. In our work, we use Hodge integrals of K-differential forms to extend quantum K-theory to a more expansive ring, relating degree-d Schubert classes to forms of degree d. This extension allows us to prove a specific relationship among these classes, generating a basis for the ring in a certain context.

The development of modern machine learning systems is driven by data and their accuracy depends on the quality of training data. However, pinpointing inaccurate data points in large datasets can be a significant challenge when testing is complete. To address this issue, we introduce a new approach to evaluating data significance in machine learning, one that builds on the Shapley value concept. By incorporating model performance into a mathematical framework that considers all possible combinations of data subsets, we develop an efficient algorithm to identify crucial data points. These data points can be isolated and used to improve the overall performance of the model. Our experiments with real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, showing a close correlation between calculated and actual model performances when using subset data. Furthermore, our method is scalable and effective even in large-scale machine learning pipelines, thanks to its flexible and modular design.

Our study investigates the sources of radio emission within Galactic globular clusters using data from 3.3 GHz observations of 57 clusters.  By applying the MAVERIC framework to our data, we identified 220 radio sources associated with globular clusters and characterized their structures.  Our results reveal that 72% of radio sources with measurable sizes have characteristics similar to those of stellar objects, while 28% have sizes comparable to those of multiple stellar entities or have undetermined sizes.  Our research also shows that radio emission within globular clusters is primarily powered by non-solar magnetic sources, as we found a correlation between radio luminosity and the spectral index, indicating a presence of plasmon sources.  By further analyzing our results, we found that radio sources with sizes comparable to multiple stellar entities are plasmon sources powered by mass accretion, while those with undetermined sizes are powered by lower mass accretion.  Our research paves the way for follow-up studies to determine the mass of these radio sources and the mass accretion rates in globular clusters.

A hypergraph consists of a collection of nodes connected by multiple edges, in contrast to regular graphs which feature single connections. Given partial information about a graph, including which nodes are linked together in a specific combination, the task of hypergraph reconstruction involves creating a complete representation of the graph. This paper focuses on the scenario where this partial information is accurate and there is an existing graph of a similar type, with the goal of developing methods to predict the complete hypergraph representation. We examine three approaches using existing graph methods, specifically hypergraph embeddings, hypergraph patterns, and a type of graph generator, and assess their performance with different levels of node connection visibility.

Our study offers an entropic analysis of directional emission in microcavity lasers. To achieve this, we utilize a minimum-entropy approach based on non-equilibrium thermodynamics. This method enables us to investigate the entropy changes associated with photon flux in multiple emission directions. Our entropic analysis shows that entropy minimization leads to beam focusing and directional emission, which is confirmed by numerical simulations. Interestingly, the entropy reduction is found to be more significant in microcavity lasers with lower $Q$ values. Our findings are also applicable to conventional lasers, where we observe that entropy reduction is less pronounced in $Q$-value optimal systems.

We examine the influence of temperature on the photonic properties of atomic ensembles, specifically focusing on thermal effects that alter the position of an excited state within the ensemble. By outlining a general framework for calculating the photon statistics of these systems, we investigate the distinct impacts of temperature on two key photonic properties: sub-poissonicity and anti-bunching. While temperature-based shifts in excited state energies significantly affect anti-bunching, our findings reveal that in certain situations, temperature can actually increase sub-poissonicity, counterintuitively enhancing the non-classical behavior of these systems.

In offline multi-agent reinforcement learning, agents train on a given dataset without interacting with the environment. This process becomes less effective as the number of agents increases, as more paths can be taken, resulting in a larger search space. We discover that in offline MARL, agents can train on a high-performing sub-set of paths, reducing the scope of their search. We develop a technique to extract this sub-set of paths and propose an algorithm to learn from it. This allows for more efficient multi-agent learning by significantly decreasing the number of actions within the search scope. In our experiments, our method achieves comparable performance to models learning from entire datasets in settings with one and two agents, and outperforms them in settings with more agents.

Megavoltage images are utilized in cancer treatment, either in 2D or 3D treatments, to locate and move tumors during radiation therapy.  The goal of this project is to develop an advanced method for aligning 2D MV images with either 3D MV images or physical measurements of the patient's position.  A new approach was tested, which involves the use of a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to match 2D images with either 3D images or patient measurement images.  The proposed system was evaluated using 60 data sets of MV images from two different cancer treatment centers, and was compared with a conventional method using only 2D projections of the 3D image.  The results showed that the new method was more accurate, with an average error of 2.8 mm, in contrast to the conventional method's error of 4.5 mm.  Notably, the proposed method was found to be highly robust, with an standard deviation of 0.7 mm, in contrast to the conventional method's higher variance of 2.3 mm.  Additionally, the project investigated the potential use of physical measurement images as a more direct and cost-effective way to validate the alignment, and showed that the error with patient measurement images was 3.5 mm.  Overall, the test demonstrated that the proposed system can efficiently and accurately align MV images, and may provide a practical and cost-effective way to validate the alignment.

If a linear combination of two or more states is entangled, it automatically results in particle steering. However, if we have a superposition of only two states, as in the Schnittcher et al. scenario, the situation becomes more complex, as no genuine multi-particle entanglement exists in this case. Consequently, this scenario highlights the inadequacy of using multi-particle entanglement as a necessary condition for steering. Moreover, this example also illustrates that single-particle entanglement alone is sufficient to generate genuine nonlocal effects, such as steering, and therefore, this aspect of entanglement should not be dismissed in any resource theory that neglects single-particle effects.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and Information and Communication Technology into the Internet of Vehicles has yielded substantial benefits, yet it also introduces critical security and privacy issues. As IoV systems handle sensitive personal information, there's a growing concern about protecting user data from unauthorized access and breaches. Presenting a robust framework that utilizes Federated Learning to secure data and a blockchain-based system for trust management could address these challenges. In this paper, we conduct an in-depth review of Federated Learning and blockchain integration in IoV, focusing on existing literature and potential solutions, but missing connections between FL and blockchain in IoV contexts are evident, requiring further exploration.

V392 Persei, classified as a dwarf nova that underwent a classic nova explosion in 2018, is an extraordinary object whose extreme evolution over nearly three years has been closely observed.  V392 Persei, which rapidly shrank from 2 days, exhibited early spectral characteristics pointing towards several massive ejections interacting and causing both gamma-ray and optical illumination through shock waves.  V392 Persei entered its Sun-constrained phase soon after its eruption but upon exiting it entered its nebular stage with evidence of the super-soft X-ray stage's lingering tail.  Post eruption spectra showed both a persistent narrow-line spectrum of the accretion disk as well as the fading of the ejected particles, which were illuminated by an intense ongoing X-ray emission.  Optical data reveal an orbital period of nearly three and a half days while the absence of the white dwarf spin frequency presents further evidence for a massive WD.  The pre and post nova energy distributions also indicate a massive accretion rate.  V392 Persei, which is located at a galactic latitude far from the plane, has a highly eccentric binary companion that V392 Persei engages in a tidal interaction that results in both curved WD edges as well as the warped of its orbit, which could have contributed to the enormous ejection seen in this system.

In quantum computing, the ability to execute multi-qubit entanglements efficiently is a key requirement, often serving as a minimum standard for a computer to be considered universal. Research has been extended to evaluate the functional capacity of quantum devices that can only perform single-qubit operations and two-qubit operations in various contexts, such as in fault-tolerant quantum computing or in quantum simulation. We examine the capabilities of quantum fault-tolerant programming using the toric code, focusing on whether two-qubit operations can suffice to execute multi-qubit operations on the code's stabilizer states. Through an analysis of the quantum circuit's resilience, we find that two-qubit operations cannot adequately support the multi-qubit entanglements required for universal quantum computation when operating on stabilizer states in the toric code. Conversely, universal quantum computation can be achieved using only two-qubit operations among different qubits.

A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach is presented, based on a Gaussian mixture model. Creating the codebook and feedback encoder involves an optimization process that minimizes the distortion of an estimated precoder, given data collected from uplink signals. Although complex, this process can be approximated using an efficient algorithm that balances performance and computational demands. Alternatively, a codebook and feedback encoder can be developed for each subband in a multi-carrier system. Additionally, an reduced feedback density welfare algorithm is introduced, enabling the exchange of codebook information between adjacent subbands.

A type of nonequilibrium, steady-state current that is robust and persistent can be found in the 3D Hofstadter model, particularly on a holographic surface with a Torus geometry. This current is protected by a symmetry similar to that which guards Dirac points in 2D Hofstadter models. We were able to mimic this effect using a 2D Hofstadter model linked to a 1D chain, and observe that the stable, steady-state current can be located near a singular point by adjusting a specific parameter. A surface with a "horse shoe" geometry can also exhibit strong, stable oscillations in both time and space if it receives a continuous flow of energy.

A model describing an accreting black hole's behavior in its immediate environment is presented, focusing on an approximately spherical area near the event horizon. This model distinguishes between two flux patterns: one that resembles a circular pattern (axisymmetric) and another that resembles a random, irregular pattern (non-axisymmetric). It shows that an axisymmetric flux pattern can support a significantly higher accretion rate than a non-axisymmetric flux pattern of the same overall energy. Specifically, a non-axisymmetric flux pattern requires at least five times more energy to achieve the same accretion rate as an axisymmetric flux pattern. This difference in accretion rates is attributed to the distinct ways matter is driven by intense electromagnetic forces within the Bondi radius. Within this radius, an axisymmetric flux pattern allows for a more localized accumulation of matter near the black hole, whereas a non-axisymmetric flux pattern leads to a scattered, irregular distribution of matter due to the distorted gravitational field. As a result, the model implies that a non-axisymmetric Bondi sphere must have a significantly more extensive overall mass inventory compared to an axisymmetric Bondi sphere with the same overall energy. It is further suggested that the observed irregularities in the disk around the black hole in GRS 1915+105 could be indicative of an exceptionally high Bondi accretion rate.

We examine the formation of Population III stars under the context of the Assembly Model, which predicts that these stars were primarily formed in nuclear star clusters at the centers of massive halos.  Using a parametric approach, we determine the basic properties of these clusters through their mass and radius, focusing on clusters with mass between $10^4$ and $10^6 M_{\odot}$.  According to the Assembly Model, Population III stars were formed in clusters located in the brightest galaxies in the early universe.  Following the collapse of their hosts and multiple mergers, these clusters were found in the heart of massive spheroidal galaxies.  Through the Assembly Model, we predict that the most massive of these clusters have the greatest abundance of Population III stars, specifically in the massive spheroidal galaxies in the present day.  These galaxies include the Milky Way and Local Group galaxies such as Andromeda.  According to the Assembly Model, the most massive of these clusters have the greatest abundance of Population III stars, specifically in the massive spheroidal galaxies in the present day.  Furthermore, it was discovered that a significant portion of these clusters have massive black holes residing in their centers, which were formed as a result of the growth of supermassive black holes in the early universe through the merger of smaller objects.  The presence of these black holes has a substantial impact on the evolution of their host clusters due to their influence on cluster potential and temperature.  Based on their mass

The Gamma-Ray Surge (GRS) detector on board the GeentComsat (GECAM) satellite is designed to monitor sudden high-energy radiation bursts. A portable GRS simulator has been developed for the purpose of testing and training the satellite's onboard GRS detectors. This simulator is capable of producing a wide range of high-energy radiation patterns, which are critical in simulating real-life radiation scenarios for the detectors. Furthermore, the simulator's portable design allows for easy use in various testing environments.

This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces, specifically on BMOA_p and its analogue VMOA_p. BMOA_p is a part of the set of F(p,q,s) spaces introduced by R. Zhao and serves as the domain for functions of positive type. VMOA_p, introduced by J. Li and Z. Chen, is equivalent to the subspace of functions with absolutely convergent series. Our article focuses on identifying the maximal semigroups of composition operators on BMOA_p and VMOA_p, as well as establishing the relationship between these semigroups and integral operators like the Hilbert and the Cauchy-type operators. We also explore how the maximal semigroups of these integral operators can be determined on BMOA_p and VMOA_p.

Humanity has continually sought knowledge, a pursuit most evident in the natural sciences where research paper output indicates the evolving state of human understanding. To navigate this information, information retrieval techniques are necessary to filter through an ever-expanding body of knowledge. However, relying solely on citation analysis, we examined three aspects of scientific productivity: researcher productivity, knowledge disparity, and research impact. We discovered that a small subset of influential scientists contributes the most to both the quantity and quality of research, while a vast majority of less influential researchers produce a minimal amount of output. Furthermore, there is a significant gap in knowledge where a small number of widely-studied topics account for most of the output, leaving many isolated areas of knowledge untouched. Interestingly, we found that the most influential researchers tend to focus on these popular topics, contributing little to the advancement of lesser-known areas. Despite the importance of resolving knowledge disparities, we found a negative correlation between a topic's information richness and the amount of further research conducted on it. Consequently, it is likely that the already well-researched topics will continue to dominate future output, implying that a wide range of knowledge remains underdeveloped.

In this study, we examine the security risks associated with wireless communication systems that use dual hop OFDM technology. To begin with, we present a general framework for analyzing the performance of AF relaying systems in fading environments. Moreover, we investigate the SE-PSR relationship of dual hop OFDM systems in various scenarios, including both co-operative and non-cooperative setups, and we investigate how certain system parameters influence the SE-PSR curve. Our research reveals that in many situations, the SE-PSR curve can be optimized in a way that maximizes the system's security and efficiency simultaneously. To validate our analytical findings, we also conduct an accompanying simulation.

Two-dimensional systems with strong inter-layer coupling, such as vertically coupled quantum layers or bilayer graphane, exhibit interconnected valance and conduction bands that can be manipulated through electrical fields. This similarity to gauge fields enables the modeling of these systems using quantum electrodynamics, allowing for the analysis of particle-like modes in these systems. In this research, we investigate the interaction between these multi-mode systems and quantum fluctuations, using waveguide quantum electrodynamics as our framework. We demonstrate that the particle-like modes in these systems can be used as both sources and detectors of quantum fluctuations. Furthermore, we showcase the ability to control the interaction between these systems and quantum fluctuations through both inter-layer coupling and electrical fields. These capabilities offer opportunities for improving the performance of quantum communication systems.

In the complex context of an urban intersection with automated and human-driven vehicles, we explore an essential challenge related to road safety: anticipating potential collisions to prevent them from happening. Our research focuses on a specific scenario where a automated vehicle approaches an intersection and must navigate through it, crossing paths with a human-driven vehicle. We develop a predictive control system capable of analyzing current and historical data to forecast how the human driver operates and where the vehicle travels. Based on these predictions, the system uses optimization techniques to determine the best course of action for the automated vehicle to minimize the risk of collision and reduce its journey time, subject to certain constraints. We test our approach on a simulated vehicle and find that it is effective in preventing collisions and minimizing delays, even in the face of varying driving speeds.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
To overcome this limitation, we present TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of TextWorld, capable of processing one million actions per second on a single GPU.
In comparison to the original TextWorld, TextWorldExpress delivers text-based gameplay at 333 times the speed, while also supporting multiple agents interacting within the same environment simultaneously.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but are hindered by their massive size, which makes them impractical for resource-constrained devices. This limitation can be addressed by LSTM-based video identification dataset reduction through a method known as Hierarchical Tucker Tensor Decomposition (HTTCD). We propose an end-to-end algorithm that combines HTTCD with a tensorized LSTM network for video identification, and an energy-efficient hardware platform for the proposed model. The algorithm is tested on the HMDB51 dataset, and our results show that it achieves comparable accuracy (73.44%) to the original dataset (73.61%) with a significant reduction in data size (from 600k to 3.5k). The accuracy of the proposed system is evaluated at different energy consumption levels, and it shows good potential for low-power operation. The hardware design of the model is implemented on a custom reconfigurable processor, and it achieves a high classification accuracy of 73.31% at a lower energy consumption of 43.36 nJ per frame.

Significant breakthroughs in machine translation have been achieved with sequence-to-sequence models, particularly those using attention and neural machine translation models. These models rely heavily on vast amounts of data, which limits their application to rare language situations. Researchers have explored methods to enhance model performance with limited data, including data augmentation techniques like back-translation and paraphrasing. We examined the effectiveness of these methods on low-resource language learning in English to Spanish and English to Hindi translation tasks. The results showed that both models performed better with data augmentation when trained on a small dataset, but only the paraphrasing model achieved comparable performance to the trained model when tested with a larger dataset. Interestingly, the hijacked model outperformed the original paraphrasing model by a large margin on the test set, but only in the English to Spanish translation task. We discovered that the hijacked model performed better when the source and target languages had similar syntax and grammar. Furthermore, we found that the hijacked model achieved better results when the test dataset has similar sentence patterns to the paraphrasing dataset. We recommend using the hijacked model for low-resource and similar language translation tasks, which could help reduce the economic barrier to entering the translation industry.

The operator that couples to a scalar in general relativity is a combination of the traceless stress tensor and a term related to the scalar curvature. This combination can be chosen such that its expectation value, when coupled to a gravitational field, minimizes the energy it contributes to the total energy of the system under certain conditions. This optimal choice leads to a more efficiently packed energy spectrum. This operator, which we call the optimal gravitational operator, behaves in a way that reflects the efficiency of this packing across different situations. For instance, its correlation length is longer than that of the stress tensor in a specific type of critical system. Additionally, this operator's matrix element, which participates in the scattering of two particles, is more efficiently distributed over possible outcomes compared to the stress tensor. This is also true for the branching ratios of decay processes. This operator's properties are related to those of the conformal primary operators in a specific theory, which form a convex set when including all possible operators that appear in the theory's spectrum. It is possible that all the properties mentioned here are a consequence of a broader principle known as the feeble gravity conjecture, which states that the optimal gravitational operator's properties will behave in a way that reflects the complexity of the system's spectrum when the gravity is weak.

To stabilize the optimization of ground and excited states on equal terms, a balanced approach is proposed, applying quantum fictitious time evolution within a model space for all states simultaneously. This method leverages the Lanczos algorithm to determine both ground and excited states by minimizing the energy variance. Two different imaginary time evolution algorithms are utilized: the one used directly for model space time-dependent Hamiltonian, and another with a projected operator for a more stable propagation. Both methods are tested on sample systems, demonstrating improved performance compared to traditional density functional theory based on time-dependent imaginary propagation.

Given a Noetherian local ring with a specific prime ideal, we consider the relationship between two invariants related to its associated prime ideals and a specific polynomial. Specifically, we examine when this polynomial, known as the tight Hilbert function polynomial, is optimal, given a specific set of conditions tied to another polynomial, specifically in relation to its reduction and ramification properties. To this end, we establish a connection between these polynomials and the geometric properties of the ring's closure within a specific algebraic variety, as well as the configuration of its associated prime ideals. We also identify a particular ring structure, namely that of reduced local Gorenstein domains, for which this tight Hilbert function polynomial is always accurate. However, we demonstrate that this property is not consistently present across all excellent local rings. Instead, we determine specific criteria under which this tight Hilbert function polynomial will be an upper bound, despite not being a perfect fit, given a particular set of prime ideals and their relationship to the ring's dimension.

A key challenge in designing policies aimed at reducing market power involves estimating the acute effects of an firm's price increase on its customers. This difficulty stems from the complex interplay of firms on interconnected markets. To address this issue, researchers often employ instrumental variable methods in a context where the firm in question operates in a single market. In contrast, this study focuses on firms with significant market presence that purchase a wide array of auxiliary services from various sellers. Following the lead of Laussel and Lemaire (1959), we employ an instrument that reflects the firm's ability to influence its own price. However, this involves a much more intricate set of interactions among firms and markets. To estimate the firm's price impact, we develop a novel model that incorporates our instrumental variable method. The model consists of a system of simultaneous equations representing the firm's price decisions and its revenue formation. Using a within-estimator approach in a setting with multiple equilibrium outcomes, we estimate the model's parameters on a dataset consisting of sales records from online auctions of advertising space. The results show that the firm's price increase leads to a substantial reduction in the number of its customers and a significant increase in the average amount paid per unit by those who remain. Moreover, we find evidence of strategic behavior among the sellers of auxiliary services, with the firm's price change affecting the number of units purchased by other firms.

Characterizing prime numbers using a given property can be viewed as an application of a more general concept that characterizes coprime numbers using that property. This characterization of primes can lead to an infinite number of statements, each representing the prime numbers meeting a specific criterion. A notable instance of such a characterization involves prime numbers that cannot be expressed as the sum of two smaller prime numbers, a criterion related to the famous twin prime conjecture. Another example is prime numbers consisting of two distinct digits, which is related to the Erdős-Sárközy conjecture. This paper explores consequences related to the Erdős-Sárközy conjecture and offers a characterizations of prime numbers consisting of two distinct digits that can be expressed as the sum of two smaller prime numbers. Additionally, this paper derives a consequence for the number of solutions to a specific polynomial equation over the complex numbers, leading to an investigation of the number of complex roots for a more general type of polynomial equation with degree four.

To study non-resonant Higgs boson pair production in the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ channel at the LHC using the matrix element method, we examine how to differentiate the Higgs boson pair signal from the dominant irreducible top quark pair background. Specifically, our analysis focuses on the 14 TeV LHC with 300 new physics toy data based on the ATLAS search for Higgs boson pair production with final states containing two bosons and two bottom quarks. By applying the matrix element method to these events, we investigate the efficiency of the selection procedure, the impact of detector simulator biases, and the ability to reject the top quark pair background while retaining a significant fraction of the signal. Our results demonstrate that approximately 0.18% of the top quark pair events are misidentified and rejected by the selection procedure, which leads to an estimated 1.53% reduction in signal events as a result of detector simulator biases. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the use of the matrix element method allows for the rejection of the top quark pair background by a factor of approximately 1.85 $\times 10^5$, or a reduction to 5.41 $\times 10^{-5}$ of the initial top quark pair background.

We calculate one-loop corrections to the Standard Model process of a Z boson emitting a Higgs boson, considering extended scalar sector scenarios for the Standard Model, including inert doublets and various triplets, quintuplets, and septuplets with different new scalar SU(2)L representations. These new scenarios are expected to be probed at a precision of a part in 10^4 by future e+e- colliders due to precise measurements of σ(e+e- → Zh) that complement searches for the Standard Model scalar sector at particle colliders such as the Large Hadron Collider, or a possible future pp collider, or Higgs decay to photons. We also find the sensitivity of σ(e+e- → Zh) and γγ decays of the Higgs boson to have the most notable complementary role in the complex triplet model scenario.

Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations of large warm whirlpools north of 75 degrees latitude. The strongest of these appear during Saturn's summer and disappear in the winter. The extensive exploration of the Saturn system with the Cassini spacecraft has provided temperature insights in the polar upper atmosphere through the use of occultations. This study makes use of these measurements to map temperature patterns in the upper atmosphere of Saturn's north polar region. The results show a significant temperature difference of around 7K when comparing the warmest and coolest areas, along with a distinct temperature gradient of around 1.5K per degree of latitude in the stratosphere. The formation of a hexagonal shape at around 75 degrees latitude in the temperature map has been identified, and it is revealed that this shape is a result of a newly formed polar vortex that is warming the surrounding air through a process of latent heat release. The formation of this vortex is believed to contribute to the formation of the temperature gradient.

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under a specific nonlinearity in $\mathbb{R}^d$ ($d\geq2$) outside a compact, convex obstacle. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse in a finite time regardless of initial conditions, provided a specific invariant manifold does not apply. Additionally, this time of collapse can be extremely brief, given certain specific angles and energies. This research extends earlier findings by D. Fournier and T. Sauer for rational potentials in $\mathbb{R}^d$ to include more general nonlinearities in $d\geq2$ (with the exception of $d=1$).

We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings for a polynomial variety defined over the integers have an equivalent form to local positive-characteristic reductions of the variety for nearly all prime numbers.

The metal-insulator transitions in V$_2$O$_3$ have been extensively studied for over fifty years with analysis of various factors influencing this phenomenon, including filming surface, pressure, and doping levels. Yet, a comprehensive understanding of the impact of surface termination in these transitions is still missing. This research delves into the mystery of the metal-insulator transitions in V$_2$O$_3$ double-unit-cell thick films, focusing specifically on changes to the surface termination from oxysulfur to oxygen. Our findings, supported by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and low-energy electron diffraction, reveal that changing the surface termination causes a shift in binding energy by approximately 0.6 eV around the critical point of the transition, and that this effect diminishes with increased distance from the transition point. Moreover, our data demonstrate that the metal-insulator transitions in V$_2$O$_3$ are influenced by the surface termination, and that this impact is comparable to that of strain and electron concentration. This study offers a fresh perspective on transitions in V$_2$O$_3$, highlighting the significance of surface modification in understanding these phenomena.

Our study uncovers new features of non-equilibrium behavior in quantum double dark-soliton states for one-dimensional repulsive boson gases. We find a specific scaling law applies to the formation of Bose-Einstein condensates in these systems as we vary both the number of particles and the size of the spatial confinement. This scaling enables us to predict the onset of a Bose-Einstein condensation at both finite sizes and in the infinite size limit. We validate our findings by calculating the condensate fraction both numerically and analytically, and the results show excellent agreement. This allows us to identify the effects of quantum fluctuations in these systems. We also examine the behavior of these systems in the equilibrium limit and find that quantum double dark-soliton states exhibit persistent non-equilibrium dynamics. This is reflected in the periodic oscillations of the condensate fraction in the large size limit. This persistence of non-equilibrium behavior is a result of the robust nature of these quantum double dark-soliton states.

We create a linearization functor for full linearization that transforms a graded bundle of degree k into a k-fold vector bundle. Our analysis determines the point at which full linearization starts to accurately capture bundle behavior, revealing that this occurs at degree 2. To demonstrate the utility of our approach, we apply it to recover Grothendieck's formula for Chern classes using the Euler characteristic of full linearizations.

This informal note begins by illustrating some technical concepts, including the re-normalization of measures and the adjustment of orbital integrals, using the algebraic closure of a local field as an example.

To analyze the chemical composition of planets beyond our current technological capabilities, a new method of detection is needed. I propose a detection system based on resonant x-ray scattering from atoms and molecules in the atmosphere of a particular planet, where it then passes through a lens made of a highly reflective material and is examined by a scanner that identifies the elemental components of the planet's atmosphere by studying the spectrum of x-rays that are reflected off the lens and space. This detection system can be used to study gas layers surrounding small bodies in the solar system and can also be used to study the atmospheric composition of exoplanets in a more refined and precise manner.

Using a realistic model of quantum error correction, which incorporates both classical and quantum errors, we derived an equivalent classical Ising model that captures the essential characteristics of these circuits. By applying this correspondence, we gained a fundamental understanding of the minimum number of non-interacting spins required in quantum error correction codes, ultimately determining the fundamental limitations imposed by symmetry constraints on code performance. Additionally, we used this framework to investigate the fundamental trade-offs between different circuit parameters affecting the correctness of quantum computations, including the interplay between number of qubits, entanglements between qubits, and error correction channels used, with our findings showing that qubits with high connectivity rates are more prone to errors when incorporating cycle-based error correction channels. Furthermore, we used this framework to explore the fundamental boundaries that cannot be overcome with further technological advancements, such as increasing the number of qubits beyond a certain point will not improve correction performance.

Recent theoretical predictions stating that group VI elemental monolayers can't be in the form of a honeycomb lattice structure have been disputed by new experimental findings. In this study, it's been found that incorporating oxygen into these monolayers, specifically tellurene, makes them dynamically stable and topologically non-trivial in the presence of strong spin-orbit coupling. Oxygen foul play is shown to push the monolayer's bandwidth into the medium range, resulting in a significant increase in its gap while maintaining the chiral edge states that characterize topological insulators. A particular oxygen functional group was discovered to produce the largest gap (around 0.36 eV) while still enabling the monolayer's 3D bulk pairing. This pairing is made possible by adjusting the Fermi level with external strain, achieving superconductivity in this material.

We develop a hybrid-mixed finite element method for single-phase Darcy flow in a fractured porous media, using a Markov chain to represent fracture connections. This approach leads to multiple non-overlapping subdomains within the fractured sections, allowing for the application of Raviart-Thomas-Nedelec mixed finite elements. A significant advantage of this method is its capability to handle the complex geometry of the fractures with minimal mesh constraints, resulting in more efficient mesh generation. We prove the method's inf-sup stability and conservativity, while also establishing an error estimate through a discrete inf-sup condition. This method is implemented using the FENICS framework and is utilized to solve a variety of test problems with increasingly complex fracture networks, showcasing its effectiveness.

A comprehensive analysis of a spin-triplet superconducting device, which involves a spiral magnetic layer and is influenced by an external magnetic field, has been conducted. A critical parameter, the critical current required for a spin-triplet superconducting effect, is found to be sensitive to the orientation of the spiral magnetic layer when the external magnetic field is strong. Additionally, there are specific magnetic configurations where a significant non-ohmic current characteristics can be induced at relatively low external magnetic fields. A spiral magnetic layer with a small pitch angle is found to be more effective in producing a large spin-triplet superconducting current.

The recent resurgence of bayes factors as a statistical hypothesis testing method has brought both praise and criticism from the research community. While bayes factors are useful for complex, nuanced decision-making, some critics argue that they are too complex for common testing scenarios. In contrast, we propose a straightforward, multi-stage approach to designing Monte Carlo simulations for bayes factor calculations. This method involves simple, robust workflow strategies for assessing the sensitivity of bayes factor results and identifying the most reliable measures of model performance. The proposed approach is accompanied by a publicly available R package called 'BFSensitivity', which demonstrates the technique and its underlying architecture.

Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. Despite their importance, the research underlying these indicators is fragmented, mainly because the existing knowledge bases lack a systematic organization of indicators, detailed analyses of sentences, and comprehensive data sets including annotations for both sentence and document levels. To address these shortcomings, we have developed DiscSense, a knowledge base that comprehensively covers a wide range of discourse indicators with diverse properties, such as "cause-effect" or "emotional response." This knowledge base is built on top of AllNLP, a universal framework that enables the creation of complex annotations for multiple indicators across large corpora. We have conducted extensive experiments to validate the performance of DiscSense on several challenging tasks, including selecting the most appropriate indicators from a list for a given sentence, pinpointing the indicators present in a sentence, identifying the indicators that best fit a document's overall meaning, and accurately predicting the annotations for both sentences and documents. These experiments have been performed on top of ArXiv, a scientific paper database, and the results have shown impressive achievements of our system across all tasks and data sets. Furthermore, we have introduced an innovative approach called DiscSense, which combines a bidirectional encoder with two separate classification modules to achieve state-of-the-art performance in semantic analysis tasks related to discourse indicators.

We investigate the spectral properties of nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond under elevated temperatures.  By developing a temperature-sensitive optical detection method, we were able to measure the concentrations of NV- centers at various temperatures between 300K and 650K.  Our results indicate that NV- centers can be accurately measured across a wide temperature range, allowing for potential applications in temperature sensing.  However, we found that NV- centers have a limited useful lifetime due to diamond degradation at higher temperatures, with optical detection accuracy degrading beyond 450K.  Nevertheless, we believe that further research could overcome these limitations, enabling the development of robust and versatile diamond sensors that can accurately measure a variety of physical parameters across a broad temperature range.

In complex neural networks, the source of training data often cannot be identified, as there is no central supervisor. In this study, a proposed model showcases the potential for a self-sustaining neural network to develop optimal performance through a mechanism reminiscent of the supergradient algorithm, achieved by combining the benefits of two processes: stochastic gradient descent within localized areas of the network, and lateral inhibitory connections between these areas. Additionally, the model's feasibility in mimicking cortical function is explored by mapping the neural components onto the structure and function of the primary visual cortex.

Using field-theoretic methods, we have developed a $\Sigma$-model that describes spin models on a triangular lattice, particularly focusing on an antiferromagnetic $SU(3)$ spin model. By making a non-degenerate perturbation in favor of antiferromagnetic arrangements, we were able to analyze the model's phase diagram and identify the parent Hamiltonian's ground states near its critical points. We found that the model's phase transition between Néel and stripe ordered phases occurs at the same critical point, $J_2 = \frac{1}{4}$, which is also where a triple-degenerate point with a ${\rm SU}(3)$ symmetry occurs. We used this approach to investigate the phase transition between two unstable, straddle-phased regions divided by stable phase boundaries, and we found that the phase transition between two straddle-phased regions occurs at $J_2 \approx 0.29$, which is not as recently reported.

A new implementation of the Hartree-Fock (HF) method has been developed to efficiently achieve robust convergence for self-consistency, utilizing a B-spline basis set that can efficiently handle complex central potentials common in physics and chemistry. This method's performance was tested with both model potentials and real atoms and ions across various stages of complexity, from hydrogen to beryllium in its ground state, and even for large, heavy elements like lead. It was found that B-spline basis set size required for self-consistency is significantly lower than that for Gaussian basis sets, particularly for larger systems where size consistency becomes a significant issue. Additionally, this new HF method was applied to full potential calculations of small metal clusters such as sodium and magnesium, yielding results that compared favorably to more limited pseudo-potential studies.

The distinction between orderly and chaotic behavior within complex systems is often determined by a single critical factor: the distance between their intrinsic time scales. However, this rule does not apply to oscillator networks, which can exhibit explosive synchronization even when there is a significant gap between the oscillators' natural frequencies. These explosive phenomena are characterized by sudden, sharp transitions from disorder to synchronization, and are often unaffected by the ratio of internal to external interactions. Using a generic, multi-frequency population model, our study reveals that explosive synchronization can occur when the difference between the longest and shortest internal time scales is smaller than the time scale of external interactions. This condition is fulfilled by populations with time scales that vary logarithmically, such as those following a power law. Our research offers a new, widely applicable framework for understanding the complex phenomena observed in oscillator networks.

We investigate a fundamental matrix optimization problem to promote low-rank structure in matrices, subject to a fixed rank that is greater than one, and provide an in-depth analysis of its landscape from a specific perspective. We show that this problem has particularly favorable properties when optimized using an appropriate method that traces the geodesic path, resulting in a convex region around the optimal solution, which indicates the absence of saddle points. We also establish a precise measure of this convex region's size, depending on the matrix in question, which potentially leads to enhanced matrix factorization performance through iterative refinement. We explore two specific applications involving matrix variate optimization, including a well-known approach to matrix completion and a novel problem to induce low-rank structure in matrices, with independent objectives for the underlying matrix and its corresponding low-rank approximation.

A graph G is considered bipartite if its vertices can be divided into two distinct groups where connections only exist between vertices within the same group. In a bipartite graph, a bicoloring can be applied by designating two distinct colors for the connected vertices. Research has shown that any connected, planar graph can be colored using a bicolored scheme, although it was hypothesized that certain planar, bipartite graphs requiring four colors for bicoloring might exist. This paper presents a bipartite graph, specifically a cubic graph, that can be bicolored with just three colors.

Let $q\ge 3$ be an integer, with $\chi$ denoting a Dirichlet character modulo $q$ and $L(s,\chi)$ being the associated Dirichlet L-functions. This paper will present specific function series, along with novel identities linking the L-functions with Gauss sums, particularly focusing on identities related to $L(2,\chi)$.

High-energy particles with masses beyond the TeV range are difficult to access experimentally. Current constraints from Big-Bang Nucleosynthesis already set a strict limit on their possible abundance, making it challenging for traditional Beyond-Standard-Model scenarios to successfully include such heavy particles in their frameworks. In contrast, our proposal takes a non-traditional approach, suggesting that these high-mass particles are not fundamental to the universe's underlying physics but rather the result of a primordial event involving the formation of long-lived cosmic strings. As these strings interact with the early universe's matter, they can periodically produce bursts of high-energy particles across a wide mass spectrum, which could explain various long-standing astrophysical phenomena.
